speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks it is, of course, too late to be original in this, but I should like to add my very sincere congratulations to those which have already been tendered in the course of this debate, to the mover and seconder in respect to the resolution on the reply to the speech from the throne, on the very excellent manner in which they discharged their duties. I particularly wish to congratulate the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mrs. Shipley) upon the fact that of all of her sex she has been the first to have the honour of moving such a resolution in this chamber. I know that her enthusiasm for her task must have been greatly heightened by the fact that this year the speech from the throne indicated the imminent passage of legislation to provide that women shall receive equal pay with men for equal work in matters coming within the federal jurisdiction. Such legislation constitutes, I think, a very significant advance in the long march towards complete recognition of women's rights. I think also the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) is to be congratulated, not only on the fact that this legislation is to be passed, but also upon the fact that it has first been given searching and careful scrutiny. It is true the principle involved seems to be simple and straightforward but I can readily see there may be many difficulties in the interpretation and application of the act when it is passed. After all, there are women concerned in this matter.
The speech from the throne confirms our knowledge that this year has been a prosperous one for Canada, and that those prophecies of depression and ruin which only a year ago echoed so freely and loudly from the opposition benches in this chamber have proved groundless. That is not to say that one can overlook the serious difficulties confronting the farming industry. It has always been my belief that prosperity in that industry is a necessary component of any stable and enduring national prosperity in this country. Therefore it is imperative that a solution be found for the difficulties which are now facing the farming population. However, this government during its tenure of office has acquired the habit of dealing effectively with all national problems which arise, and I am confident that it will take every feasible and desirable step within its power to deal successfully with this problem also, and not only the vexing problem of agricultural surpluses, but also the allied one of undue disparity between agricultural prices and cost of production.
Apropos of the western wheat problem, I might say, Mr. Speaker, this matter is being dealt with very ably by speakers from the
208	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Lusby government benches, and I do not feel called upon to speak about it myself. However, in passing, I noticed the other day that when the Leader of the Opposition was speaking in this debate he suggested that certain low grade western wheat should be sold as feed grain in Ontario, Quebec and abroad. Those are his words as I got them from Hansard.
I should like to point out to the Leader of the Opposition that there are many farmers in the maritimes who are also substantial users of feed grains, and who have benefited greatly by the policy adopted by this government of granting freight assistance for the movement of western feed grains to eastern Canada, which includes the maritimes. Surely, Mr. Speaker, in any scheme to dispose of this low grade western wheat, the maritimes should be considered. I do not think any movement of that wheat eastward should stop in Ontario or Quebec.
In the field of external affairs the need, stressed in the speech from the throne, to maintain a strong North Atlantic Treaty Organization as part of an effective defence system cannot be too strongly urged, and it is my hope that while the military aspects of NATO are developed its economic aspects and implications will not be neglected. Among the organization's aims is the co-operative fostering and strengthening of the economic life of its member states, and today, with the effective waging of war so largely based upon industrial strength, a strong economy is as essential to any nation for defence as a large army or modern air force. Effective defence is closely geared to the economic strength of a nation. Moreover, an impoverished economy in any nation is a direct invitation to communism.
I should also like to commend the government upon its decision to give continued support to the United Nations. And in this connection I wish particularly to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) upon the important role he played in obtaining the recent admission of additional nations to UN membership. To my mind, one of the marked weaknesses of the United Nations has lain in the fact that, with so many qualified states denied admission, it was not truly a representative world organization. The recent increase in its membership has done much to alleviate this situation, and should add greatly to the stature of the organization as a working instrument for the preservation of world peace. The minister can take justifiable pride in the fact that the Canadian delegation, under his guidance, led the way in bringing about this favourable result.


In this debate, Mr. Speaker, the contributions of most members are in part at least a sort of "state of the constituency" message, and I naturally wish to observe the custom by placing before this house some of the needs and aspirations of my own constituency.
In my constituency of Cumberland, Mr. Speaker, the year has been generally a good one, although our farmers have been confronted by difficulties, as have farmers elsewhere. Lumbering and industrial activity has continued at satisfactory levels. The coal mining industry, which, of all our industries, is to me the cause of most concern, has held its own, with the prospect that it can continue to do so, although the seasonal lack of orders during the warm weather months remains a problem for the smaller, independent mine operators.
Here let me say, Mr. Speaker, that while the long-range prospects for our Nova Scotia coal industry encourage no undue optimism, the fact that there has been some improvement during the year indicates the importance to the industry of a high level of industrial activity in Canada generally. Given that, our coal industry may face the future with greater confidence. For example, in my own town of Amherst, which is an industrial town, the high level of industrial activity which I may say has been aided substantially by orders and contracts from this government, has been of very material benefit to the Cumberland coal mining industry.
In this connection also, I should like to suggest to this government that the development of our Canadian steel industry, that great user of coal, particularly in eastern Canada, would be of incalculable benefit to our coal industry and I believe could prove its ultimate salvation. It would certainly remove to a large extent the cloud of uncertainty which still hangs over the future of the industry. Of course, the freight subventions paid by this government, including those of the past year, which were successfully designed to aid Nova Scotia coal in finding a sales outlet in Great Britain and continental Europe, have remained a chief prop of the industry.
I should like to suggest that this government co-operate in every possible way with the provincial governments concerned in an effort to implement the recommendations contained in the Christie report, which envisages the widespread production and distribution of electrical power throughout the maritimes produced by a system of coal-burning steam plants. In my opinion, in the production of electrical power by the use of coal-fired steam plants lies the true future of maritime electrical development, far more than in any hydro development that could be contemplated.

I have said that in my constituency this year has generally been a good one, but in Nova Scotia and in fact throughout the mari-times we need something more than an assurance of a good year. I think more than any other part of Canada we need the assurance of a good future, a stable and prosperous future. Today it borders on the trite to say that, economically and otherwise, Canada has a brilliant and prosperous future. For the country as a whole and for the more fortunate provinces that is entirely true, but if that future is to be brilliant and propitious in every respect, then we must be able to apply that saying with equal aptness to every province of this dominion.
While I do not suggest at the present time that we in the maritimes are facing the future with any pessimism, because we certainly are not, yet we are well aware that, regrettably, and so far inescapably, we are more vulnerable to any adverse economic winds that may begin to blow than any other part of Canada.
It has been said by the Prime Minister that there is a growing spirit of Canadian unity. Again, that is perfectly true, but if that spirit is to reach full fruition efforts must be put forth to ensure that every province of this federated country shall share in an equitable degree in the prosperity and development of the country as a whole. There is nothing more conducive to a spirit of disunity, or at least a spirit of apartness, than the existence of a pronounced gap between the prosperity and economic level of certain provinces and the prosperity and economic level of other provinces. While substantial gains have been made in the less favoured provinces in raising their economic levels, the gap does remain substantial. I think that every effort should be made to see that every province shall enjoy fully an adequate economic level as compared with any other province.
What should be the role of the federal government in this regard? In spite of the somewhat chilling influence of the British North America Act, the concept of the federal government as a significant factor in the economic life of this country has broadened vastly since the days of confederation. Always, of course, the federal government has been accustomed to act within its own jurisdictional fields, as defined by that act, not only to protect the interests of Canada as a whole, but to undertake, wherever real need may exist, such useful projects as fall within those fields, even though primarily calculated to create benefits of merely provincial or at most regional scope. I refer to such things as harbour improvements in Halifax or the building of a canal in Ontario. Nor has this
The Address-Mr. Lusby restriction of the benefits in such cases to provincial or regional scope been in itself deemed a valid objection to federal action within federal fields of jurisdiction.
In more recent times, however, we have seen a far-reaching extension of federal activity, sometimes with provincial participation, sometimes without, sometimes with the sanction of a constitutional amendment, sometimes without, into fields where the venerable fathers of confederation, even if they could have envisaged the subjects at all, would never have expected the federal government to poke its nose. There are many instances of this, such as unemployment insurance and assistance, old age assistance, blind and disability pensions, indeed the whole realm of social security. In addition there are such things as the trans-Canada highway, disaster relief and public health. In my opinion these are all prime examples of that slow extension of federal activity into broader and broader fields of national life. In each case, of course, federal participation has been explained by the fact that it is deemed to be a matter of national interest or concern and that to deal with the subject adequately is beyond the available provincial resources.
In my opinion, the over-all effect of these extensions of federal activity and the resulting greater impingement of that activity upon the economy of the country has been to lessen the gap which exists between the economic levels of the less fortunate provinces and those of the more fortunate and therefore to foster in no small degree that spirit of national unity which, as the Prime Minister has said, is indeed growing and steadily knitting this country into a true national entity, however diverse its components.
But the gap, the disparity between the economic levels of the two classes of province, still remains substantial, far too much so. I submit that the federal government should undertake, not tentatively, not sporadically, but as a matter of settled and continuing national policy, the narrowing of that gap, the lessening of that disparity, by every feasible means at its command. Thereby can be achieved a signal contribution to the cause of Canadian unity and true future greatness.
Let me suggest one way in which this government may within its own established constitutional sphere advance such a policy. I think it is generally agreed that the vast concentration of industry in certain restricted areas of the country is to be deprecated. I do not think that anyone would wish to have all industry concentrated in two or three or four small areas of a country. Of course, no one will question the right of the industrialist to locate his plant wherever he considers it most

The Address-Mr. Lusby advantageous to do so, but it seems to me that a proper system of allocation of government contracts and orders could be used so that those regions which are most in need of industrial building up would be encouraged. If that were done, not only would those regions, -and of course the maritimes are one of them, -which require greater industrial activity be encouraged to build up their industrial economies; it would also to some degree tend to halt or at least slow down the existing concentration of industry in areas already overdeveloped.
When I say that the government should adopt as a national policy the task of lessening the economic gap between different provinces, it seems to me that this may, and probably would, involve further advances by the federal government into spheres of activity that hitherto have perhaps been considered purely provincial preserves: a greater degree of federal participation and assistance in projects which, in the past at least, would have been considered of only provincial concern. Undoubtedly here constitutional problems cannot be ignored, and, of course, there are many provincial rights and privileges which must be jealously guarded. I am certainly not one to advocate the destruction of any essential provincial rights. Nonetheless, I do submit that the British North America Act, which is the foundation stone of our constitution, never was intended to be in the nature of a strait-jacket against legitimate Canadian development, certainly not a rack upon which the economy of any one province should be warped.
The Prime Minister has very properly said that this government must be most careful in expending in any one province moneys raised from the Canadian taxpayers as a body. Certainly such caution is required; nor do I advocate any wholesale federal participation in purely provincial projects. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) this morning propounded a list of questions to which he said the Prime Minister had answered no. There is one question to which the Prime Minister and this government have always said no, and that is to the question, "Will you countenance any wasteful or inexpedient expenditure of public moneys?"
I hope they will continue at all times to say no to that question. Nonetheless, if in any of the less favoured provinces there is some useful project which would have the effect of substantially promoting the economic life

of that province, and if the financial resources of that province are not adequate to carry the load, I submit that then federal participation in such a project should be deemed legitimate and proper and that, above all, the question of such participation should be faced boldly and not with any undue constitutional qualms. As for the Canadian taxpayers, a wise and sound application of such a policy would in the end prove for them the old story of bread upon the waters.
Turning again to my own province and constituency, I note that there is no mention in the speech from the throne of any specific federal or joint federal-provincial undertaking in Nova Scotia. That is hardly surprising in view of the fact that a number of such projects have only recently been completed, ranging from the Canso causeway to the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry service. Yet I hope that in the not far distant future some speech from the throne will foreshadow the appointment of a royal commission to inquire with the utmost detail into the feasibility, the cost and the economic benefits to be legitimately expected from the construction of a canal across the isthmus of Chignecto.
This matter has been broached in the past and was broached earlier in this debate by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy). I myself have spoken about it on numerous occasions and, like him, I shall continue to do so. I have never been one of those who take the view that we should build the canal first and then discuss the probable economic benefits afterwards. In common with most of those who have given some attention and study to the project, I am reasonably confident that a thorough investigation into the matter by a royal commission would give a favourable answer to the question whether the economic benefits to be derived by the Atlantic provinces, and indeed by Canada as a whole, would justify the expenditures which would be entailed. If that question were once favourably answered, I am confident that the construction of the Chignecto canal would not be long delayed. Certainly the people of the maritimes are entitled to have that question considered and to have it answered definitively once and for all. I therefore urge again the appointment of a royal commission to investigate the matter in its every aspect and to answer that question. I hope and believe the answer will be a favourable one.

The Chignecto canal, when constructed, will lie upon or close to the northern border of my constituency, which, as many know, is connected with the neighbouring New Brunswick constituency of Westmorland by the isthmus of Chignecto, which is of great importance in that it links the mainland of North America to Nova Scotia. If we cross my constituency to the southern side-that is, the Minas basin shore-we find there at the present time a pressing need for another transportation link: the re-establishment of a ferry service from the Cumberland county shore across Minas basin to the Kings county shore. Here a short water trip of approximately seven miles would obviate for commercial and other road traffic a trip around the head of that body of water of some 20 times the distance. Consequently, as a stimulus to commercial road traffic between the Annapolis valley and Cumberland county, eastern and northern New Brunswick, and even so far afield as Quebec and Montreal, that ferry link would be of inestimable benefit. To the tourist trade it would be a natural complement to the Yarmouth-Bar Harbor ferry service which has been recently established. Yet, after many years of operation, that ferry service was discontinued during the last war, and it has not been resumed, in spite of the vastly greater need for it today than ever existed before.
A strong and vigorous association, the Minas basin ferry association, has now been formed to press for assistance in re-establishing this service. The cost of deep water terminals which would enable the ferry, unlike its predecessors, to operate at all stages of the tide, will undoubtedly be substantial. Although I have no doubt that the provincial government would strongly favour this project, yet it may well be that it will fail for lack of financial means unless a measure of federal aid is forthcoming. It is my earnest hope that any representations of the Minas basin ferry association to Ottawa in this connection-and I hope they will be fortified, as I expect they will be, by all available facts and figures to prove the extent of the advantages to the economy of Nova Scotia and the maritimes-will meet with a favourable reception here.
I am aware that, unlike the Chignecto canal, which is a matter entirely within the jurisdictional responsibility of the federal government, the Minas basin ferry service, since it is projected to operate only between two points in the one province, is in a somewhat different category.
The Address-Mr. Lusby
Our old friend the British North America Act expressly places ferries operating between two provinces or between Canada and another country within the federal orbit of jurisdiction, but I believe that its silence with regard to ferries operating only between points in one province has been interpreted by our courts as meaning that the latter type of ferry falls within the provincial sphere.
Yet is it not somewhat illogical, Mr. Speaker, to suggest that if the Minas basin ferry happened to operate across the headwaters of the bay of Fundy, let us say, to some point in New Brunswick, it would be a legitimate object of federal bounty, while if it operated only between two points in Nova Scotia it would not be? After all, one of the primary objects of the ferry service would be to promote trade between the Annapolis valley and points in New Brunswick, definitely interprovincial trade. As I said, it would shorten the trucking route very substantially.
Here, I think, is a striking opportunity to apply the principle I was advocating a few moments ago, that if a project will have the effect of materially strengthening the economy of one of the less favoured provinces, yet the project will fail without federal assistance because of lack of provincial financial resources, that project should be a legitimate object of federal participation. There are precedents for subsidies to ferries operating only between provincial points, and in fact prior to its discontinuance during the war this particular ferry enjoyed a modest federal subsidy, though possibly the constitutional question was skirted to some extent there by the fact it was then operated by the Dominion Atlantic Railway, which is a subsidiary of the C.P.R.
In any event, jurisdictional question or not, the matter of federal aid in the re-establishment of this ferry service is certainly one deserving of the most careful and sympathetic consideration, and I earnestly ask that it be given such consideration whenever it is brought to the attention of the government.
There were one or two other matters I wished to mention in connection with my constituency, but I think I will simply refer to one more, the matter of the program of building armouries. This of course concerns the Department of National Defence. I understand there is a need for new armouries at many points in the maritime provinces, and I am particularly concerned about the town of Springhill, which had a very fine record
212	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blair during the last war, and indeed during both wars. Its sons joined the colours freely, fought bravely, and the muster roll of the dead and wounded is very great for a town of that size. The people there support militia training very strongly, yet there is only an old wooden building which serves as an armoury and is most inadequate for the purpose. True, it was fixed up. It was condemned a year or so ago and some money was spent in repairing it. I suppose the militia can carry on with it, but certainly it is not the type of accommodation they should have.
I understand there are many other places where there are perhaps no armouries at all, and that the allotment of funds under the armoury building program is such that it will be years before the program is completed.
I think we are all agreed that the problem of national defence is going to continue for years to come as one of the foremost problems of the government. We know that the Geneva spirit evaporated. Personally I never had any expectation that it would do otherwise. For the foreseeable future Canada is going to have to maintain immense armaments and be ready for any eventuality. Surely if that is the case and men are to be trained against the prospect of war they are entitled to every facility to enable them to become efficient soldiers.
Therefore I urge the Department of National Defence to enlarge and hasten the program of building armouries, for after all an armoury is a very important part of the training of the militia. I urge that the program be speeded up, and I sincerely hope that in the very near future the town of Springhill will be provided with a fully adequate armoury.
Mr. W, G. Blair (Lanark): Mr. Speaker, I first wish to add my words of congratulation to the mover (Mrs. Shipley) and seconder (Mr. Laflamme) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Their speeches were well delivered and well prepared.
It is an unusual fact, sir, that exactly a year ago today at about this time in the afternoon I had the pleasure of following the hon. member who has just completed his speech. There have been many subjects under consideration in this debate and many problems have been presented to the house. The problem I wish to present to hon. members today is the problem of the agriculturists, not only in my own constituency of Lanark but in the Dominion of Canada as a whole.

Yesterday the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) placed before the house the condition of the cheese producers in his own riding and in the province of Ontario generally. I find myself in complete agreement, because in the speech I made a year ago to which I have referred I dealt with this very same matter. I reached the same conclusions; therefore I congratulate him on the speech he has presented to the house dealing with that question.
I am also well aware that there is a problem in the Canadian west in connection with the disposal of wheat, a problem that is apparently causing hardship to the farmers. I am aware that the marketing of wheat is important to the whole economy of Canada. In dealing with the question of dairy products today may I say that I have not changed my position with regard to the importation of New Zealand cheese. I find there is a desire even in my own riding that some form of protection should be afforded the dairy farmers, and they have even asked for protection on cheese at the rate of so much per pound.
But I wish today to take up the question of butter and the surpluses existing in Canada at the present time. This is another problem of the dairy industry that we had last year. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has consistently pointed out that there is no surplus of butter, and I might say he couples with that the statement that if we sell ten or twelve million pounds there will be no surplus of butter in Canada.

I note that on December 23 in a letter to the Winnipeg Tribune the Minister of Agriculture sought to clarify his viewpoint, and he stated at that time:
I said in every statement I have made that after we have sold ten to twelve million pounds of butter there will be no real surplus in Canada. We require what is left to have a sufficient supply of butter at all points across the country.
It does seem odd to me that we will have no surplus if we get rid of ten or twelve million pounds. Yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in a very optimistic speech to the house-and I have no doubt he has grounds for his optimism- pointed out the heavy demand for such commodities as iron, copper and nickel. This will have little bearing on the financial condition

of the farmers in my riding, where one of the chief occupations is dairy farming.
I find the position of the Minister of Agriculture difficult to understand in view of his persistent statement that there is no surplus, when reputable statistics reveal a surplus varying anywhere from 50 to 60 million pounds. It is a peculiar fact that speeches made either by himself or by others interested seem to take a certain line. We even find such statements made by officials of his own department. This line seems to take the following viewpoint:	"The production and the
consumption of butter are gradually getting closer together."
We hear that on all sides. It may be that in the long run they are getting closer together. We may be approaching the place where the production of butter may be equal to the domestic consumption, but we are a long way from that position. This result could only be achieved by an increase in the population of this country of possibly several million people. At the rate people are coming into this country-at rates accomplished by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, judged by last year's figures-that period is many years away.
The Minister of Agriculture has attempted to place himself in a position-at least it seems that way to me-wherein any attempt to criticize this surplus might be regarded as unpatriotic. First he points out that a certain amount is required for pipe-line needs. I think we would all agree in this house that we have had enough controversial debates about pipe lines without bringing in the butter situation. But at all events he points out the need for a supply of butter to the consumers. Then he points out that a large amount of butter is required for stabilization. That large amount of butter is somewhat indefinite. He points out that any amount is not surplus. His position is simply this. There is no surplus after we get rid of the surplus. You remember the old saw; if we had some bacon and if we had some eggs, we could have eggs and bacon.
Let us consider the position in Canada at the present time. The Canadian government floor price on butter is 58 cents per pound. The sale made to Czechoslovakia was at 37 cents a pound. But at the time that sale was made-the house was sitting last June and July-vigorous protests were made about the sale at that price to the communists. In the meantime New Zealand has protested to Canada against sales of this type. Since last
The Address-Mr. Blair fall the Canadian government has protested to the United States with regard to the United States policy of wheat marketing. New Zealand has now accused Canada of being guilty of the same sort of thing with butter as the United States is doing with wheat. The Canadian government has given assurance to New Zealand that our sales of butter on the world market would not be injurious to New Zealand trade. It is therefore apparent that in the government's policy there is some conflict between the marketing of butter and the marketing of wheat.
As I said, the first sale of butter to Czechoslovakia was in July of 1955. One must note that it was sold for export at a lower price than the market value here. It therefore did not interfere with the world price, which at that time was about 41 cents a pound. The cost of shipment in this case will be 3 cents a pound, and another 3 cents could be allowed if it were necessary for making it salt-free.
Another opportunity arose in November to sell eight million pounds to East Germany. In this case the price was 37 cents, which could be considered the London price less the cost of shipping. This month there is a further sale of one million pounds to Czechoslovakia at 39 cents a pound, but a new factor has entered into the business and that is probably the cause of the protest which New Zealand has made. I refer to the fact that there has been a rise in the world price of butter of about 9 cents a pound in the last few weeks. The price in London is now approximately 48 or 49 cents for Australian butter, slightly higher for New Zealand butter, and again a slightly higher rate for Danish butter. These are the sales which the government has made in an attempt to get rid of its so-called surplus. In view of all the statements that have been made the question arises, what is the amount of surplus butter on hand?
The province of Manitoba has entered into the dispute. Their department of agriculture has made a statement to the effect that the real surplus of butter amounts to about 50 million pounds. The national dairy council of Canada gives a much higher figure. Based on dominion bureau of statistics data I was able to work out the following statistics, and I should like to present them to the house. This is a table of dairy production and consumption trends. First we consider the livestock population of this country as of June 1, the number of milk cows on the farm.
